# Halve bulletSpeed in unknown-archetype fallbacks

## Problem statement

AH-0MUWZ5GST003NMFQ halves the enemy `bulletSpeed` of the eight shipped archetypes
across the runtime CSV, `DEFAULT_ENEMY_CONFIGS` and the per-entity constants.
During planning, three additional runtime fallbacks were found that also hard-code
`bulletSpeed: 200` for **unknown** archetype keys and were explicitly out of that
item's scope (its Q2 enumeration covered only CSV + defaults + entity constants):

- `src/core/configStore.ts` — `genericEnemyDefault()`
- `src/core/difficultySequencer.ts` — `resolveBaseConfig()`
- `src/core/enemyDifficulty.ts` — `groupEnemyConfig()`

Leaving them at 200 means an unknown-key enemy would fire at double the speed of
every shipped archetype, so tuning can still drift for that edge case.

## Desired change

Decide and, if accepted, halve these three `bulletSpeed` fallbacks (200 → 100) for
consistency, updating any affected difficulty-sequencer expectations.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC1 — The three unknown-archetype fallbacks use `bulletSpeed: 100` (or a
  documented decision is recorded to leave them at 200 with rationale).
- [ ] AC2 — Any difficulty-sequencer or difficulty-scoring test affected by the
  change is updated and the full suite passes.
- [ ] AC3 — The decision and rationale are recorded on this item.

## Key Files

- `src/core/configStore.ts`
- `src/core/difficultySequencer.ts`
- `src/core/enemyDifficulty.ts`

- AH-0MUWZ5GST003NMFQ — Reduce bullet speed of enemies (parent discovery; strictly out of its scope).

## Problem

Several deterministic bot micro-simulations are knife-edge calibrations: a subtle, legitimate gameplay tweak (e.g. the 1-5% gentler thrust-press reduction in AH-0MUYRJQE50021T4A) flips their outcomes because scores are dominated by discrete hit/bullet collisions.

During AH-0MUYRJQE50021T4A two tests had to be recalibrated:
- src/ai/style/evaluation.test.ts - synthetic human seed moved 7 -> 14.
- src/ai/framework/competent/competentBot.integration.test.ts - RUN_SEED moved 0x0b07 -> 0x0b16.

On the base behaviour, src/ai/style/evaluation.test.ts already regressed on 13/24 seeds, and the competent-vs-legacy AC6 test only wins in base because the legacy bot chaotically collides with bullets; without bullets the legacy bot scored higher (22 vs 20) on base.

## Goal

Make these tests robust rather than seed-picked:
- Aggregate competence/style comparisons over a set of seeds (e.g. assert the styled/competent bot is not systematically worse), or
- Compare on scenarios whose score is not dominated by discrete collisions.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: The style-match AC4 demonstration no longer depends on a single lucky seed (e.g. asserts over multiple seeds).
- AC2: The competent-vs-legacy AC6 test asserts an objective-based advantage rather than relying on chaotic bullet collisions.
- AC3: Recalibrating either test is not required by an unrelated small bot-feel tweak.
- AC4: Full test suite, typecheck and build pass.

# Enemies should be aware of the wrap around

## Problem statement

Enemies are currently "wrap-blind": aimed shots always fire a straight line at
the player's raw position (never crossing a screen edge), and enemy movement is
bounded or clamped to the arena, so no enemy ever flies over a screen edge the
way the player ship, asteroids, bullets and the raider patrol already do. The
playfield seam is therefore one-directional — only the player's shots and the
player can cross it — letting the player camp the edges with impunity. Enemy
behaviour should be wrap-aware by default — firing across the seam to reach the
player and flying over the edges — controlled by a per-enemy parameter so a
small set of classic arcade archetypes (Space Invaders march, Centipede) keeps
its bounded, wall-respecting behaviour.

## Users

- **Players** — enemy shots can now arrive from anywhere, including from
  "off-screen" across the seam, so camping a screen edge is no longer a safe
  position. Most enemies occupy the whole wrap-around world rather than a
  bounded box, while the classic set pieces (Space Invaders, Centipede) stay
  recognisible.
- **AI agents / human developers** — one unambiguous data-driven per-archetype
  parameter (`wrapAware`, default `true`) that the game and every gym read
  through the same shared seams, so game↔gym parity is preserved by
  construction and tuning an archetype is a one-field change.

### Example user stories

- As a **player**, I want enemies to fire at me across the screen edge, so that
  hiding against an edge is no longer a guaranteed safe position and shots can
  arrive from the seam exactly like my own wrapped bullets.
- As a **player**, I want most enemies to fly over a screen edge and reappear on
  the opposite side, so the whole wrapped playfield — not a bounded box — is
  part of the arena.
- As a **player**, I want the Space Invaders block and the Centipede to keep
  their classic behaviour (reversing at the walls / weaving within the arena),
  so those recognisable set pieces remain intact.
- As a **developer**, I want a single data-driven `wrapAware` parameter per
  archetype (default: aware) that behaves identically in the game and every
  gym, so enabling or disabling seam-awareness is a one-field change with no
  divergent copies.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. **Parameter** — Each enemy archetype carries a data-driven boolean
   `wrapAware` (or equivalently named) parameter, defaulting to `true`, wired
   through the existing `EnemyConfig` pipeline so it is visible and editable in
   the enemy editor panel. The `march` (Space Invaders) and `centipede` seed
   configs set it to `false`.
2. **Seam-aware aimed fire** — Aimed shots (Scout, march and the raider's
   aimed fire — every archetype routed through the aimed-shot method) fire
   along the shortest wrapped path to the player: when the direct line is
   longer than the wrap-around route, the shot leaves one edge and arrives from
   the opposite edge (enemy bullets already wrap; AH-0MU960UTE001PTV0). An
   enemy with `wrapAware: false` keeps the current direct aim.
3. **Wrap-aware movement** — Wrap-aware enemy motion (dive, chase, orbit,
   drift, roam, hold-and-move, etc.) that would carry the enemy off-screen
   wraps to the opposite edge (matching the player/asteroid four-edge wrap
   model) instead of being clamped. Non-aware archetypes (`march`,
   `centipede`) are unchanged: march reverses and drops at the arena edge;
   centipede weaves within bounds.
4. **Gym ↔ game parity** — The behaviour is implemented once in the shared
   core (`src/scenes/core/`) and exercised by the affected gym scene(s) and
   `PlayScene` in the same change, so the repo-wide duplicate-body / parity
   guards stay green.
5. **Testing, validation & docs** — Unit tests cover: seam-aware aim angle for
   wrap-aware enemies vs. direct aim for non-aware enemies; position wrapping
   on crossing each edge for wrap-aware motion; config default / CSV wiring
   including the `march` / `centipede` exclusions. The affected documentation
   (`docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md` and any config-format docs) is
   updated to reflect the change. The full project test suite passes with the
   new changes.

## Constraints

- Do not change the bullet wrap model itself — enemy bullets already wrap and
  expire by lifetime (AH-0MU960UTE001PTV0); this item changes launch direction
  and enemy movement only.
- Exclusions are an explicit seed-config list: only `march` and `centipede`
  default to non-aware. During planning, any other archetype whose classic
  design requires wall interaction belongs in the exclusion list, recorded as a
  code comment and a documented divergence per the gym↔game parity convention
  (AH-0MUGZDTFX004RBD1).
- Implement through the shared core (`src/scenes/core/`), never a divergent
  copy, so the game and every gym run the same code.
- Out of scope: boss behaviours, player ship, minerals, drops, and the bullet
  wrap model itself.
- Written in UK English per repo convention.

## Existing state

- Enemy aimed fire: `Scout.tryFireAimedBullet` computes
  `heading = atan2(target.y - y, target.x - x)` on **raw** positions with no
  seam consideration — the same aimed-shot method is reused for march and
  raider via `ENEMY_FIRE_METHODS` (`src/entities/enemyFire.ts`).
- Enemy bullets: wrap all four screen edges and expire by lifetime
  (AH-0MU960UTE001PTV0; shared bullet path in `src/entities/PlayerBullet.ts`).
- Enemy movement: bounded. Ghost/Grunt clamp to `GAME_WIDTH`/`GAME_HEIGHT`;
  march reverses and drops at arena bounds (`src/scenes/core/marchFormation.ts`:
  `computeMarchBounds` / `advanceMarch`); centipede weaves within bounds;
  formation drift pushes rightward.
- Wrap model to match: player ship and `Asteroid.updatePosition` four-edge
  wrap; `Raider` patrol already wraps; `LaneTraffic` wraps horizontally.
- Enemies are data-driven: `EnemyConfig` (`src/core/configTypes.ts`) + seed
  defaults (`src/core/configDefaults.ts`) + CSV (`src/data/enemy-configs.csv`)
  + enemy editor panel + gym editor.

## Desired change

1. Add the boolean parameter to `EnemyConfig` (`wrapAware`), seed default
   `true`; set `march` and `centipede` to `false`.
2. Seam-aware aim: for wrap-aware entities, compute the player delta along the
   shortest wrapped path before `atan2` in the shared aimed-fire seam; used by
   Scout / march / raider aimed fire (and any other archetype sharing the
   aimed-shot method).
3. Shared post-motion edge wrap: in the shared scene entity loop (game +
   gyms), wrap each wrap-aware enemy's position when it crosses an edge; gate
   on the flag so non-aware archetypes are untouched.
4. Verify per-archetype that nothing breaks (divers mid-dive, chasers,
   orbiters, swarm, formation drift) and adjust tests.
5. Update key docs (`docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md`; config-format
   docs if they enumerate fields).

## Key Files

- `src/core/configTypes.ts` — add `wrapAware?: boolean` to `EnemyConfig`.
- `src/core/configDefaults.ts` — seed defaults: `true` for most archetypes;
  `false` for `march` and `centipede`.
- `src/data/enemy-configs.csv` — new `wrapAware` column entries (if the CSV
  persists the field).
- `src/entities/enemyFire.ts` + aimed-fire call sites (`Scout.tryFireAimedBullet`,
  march, `Raider`) — seam-aware aim.
- `src/entities/BaseEnemy.ts` — expose the flag and any shared seam support.
- `src/scenes/core/` — shared post-motion wrap (CombatCoreScene / CombatScene
  shared entity loop, alongside the `enemyTargeting.ts` seams).
- `src/scenes/gym/core/GymFormationScene.ts` + affected gym scenes
  (`GymFodderEnemies`, `GymCentipede`, …) — parity exercises.
- `docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md` — document the parameter and the
  exclusions.

## Risks & assumptions

- **Risk: gameplay feel** — seam-aware aimed fire lets shots come from
  unexpected directions; mitigated by limiting the change to aimed shots
  (radial/spread remain direction-symmetric) and excluding the classic
  archetypes.
- **Risk: wrap × state-machine interaction** — a post-motion wrap applied to
  every wrap-aware archetype could interact with steering that seeks the player
  or with dive/common state machines near the seam (oscillation). Mitigation:
  per-archetype verification during planning and dedicated unit tests at the
  seam.
- **Risk: formation-drift scope** — drift formations that push off-screen wrap
  at the entity level; formation *bases* and shaping logic stay as-is.
- **Scope-creep guard** — seam-aware spread/radial patterns (Q2 option b) are
  out of scope; if wanted later they are tracked as a new work item, not added
  here. Any extra archetype exclusion discovered during planning becomes a new
  work item or is documented as a divergence, not silent scope growth.
- **Assumption: config plumbing** — the parameter lives in `EnemyConfig`
  (CSV-backed, editor-editable), consistent with the established data-driven
  enemy tooling; default `true` for all archetypes except the explicit
  exclusions.

## Related work

- **AH-0MU960UTE001PTV0** — "Bullets should have a distance and should wrap
  around the screen" (completed). Bullets already wrap; this item builds
  directly on that model for launch direction.
- **AH-0MV8BSMXC0097KLW** — "Enemies should emerge from the wormhole" (open).
  Touches the same shared enemy spawn/motion seams; potential overlap to watch
  during planning.
- **AH-0MU4KQ6NT006MP52** — "Extract common enemy base class for regular
  enemies" (completed). `BaseEnemy` hosts the shared config/seam support.
- **AH-0MTFP7EIC004F1MN** — "Enemy Design tooling" (completed). The
  data-driven `EnemyConfig` pipeline this parameter extends.
- **AH-0MTAN4X5D009D7U6** — "Write ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md
  best-practice guide" (completed). The doc updated by AC 5.
- **AH-0MUGZDTFX004RBD1** — gym↔game parity convention (referenced in
  `AGENTS.md`), enforced by `CombatScene.equivalence.test.ts`.

## Appendix: Clarifying questions & answers

- Q1: "Movement scope: which enemies should actually 'fly over the edge'? (a)
  All wrap-aware archetypes — shared post-motion wrap in scene loops;
  march/centipede excluded. (b) Firing only. (c) A curated subset."
  — Answer (Map): "(a)". Source: interactive reply, intake round 1.
- Q2: "Firing scope: which fire patterns become seam-aware? (a) Aimed shots
  only. (b) All patterns."
  — Answer (Map): "(a)". Source: interactive reply, intake round 1.

# Audio Design Chapter — retro-arcade survival game GDD

## Problem statement

The GDD currently defines only SFX (§7.3 Audio Direction) and states background music is out of MVP scope with no musical direction defined. The game lacks a documented musical identity (scales, motifs, harmonic language, instrumentation, dynamic mixing, and state-driven music architecture) to guide composition and implementation when music is eventually built.

## Users

- **Audio designers and composers** — need a definitive musical language (scales/modes, motifs, progressions, instrumentation palette) to write consistent, on-brief music.
- **Technical audio programmers** — need the implementation contract (bus architecture, priority tiers, ducking, state machine, middleware guidance) to build or integrate the music system.
- **Game designers / producers** — need per-game-state emotional targets and transition rules to keep audio aligned with gameplay pacing.

User stories:

- As an audio designer, I want documented scales and motifs per game state, so my compositions match the game's emotional arc without guesswork.
- As a technical audio programmer, I want the music state machine and dynamic-mixing rules defined, so I can implement or configure the music engine against a fixed contract.
- As a producer, I want music explicitly scoped as design reference (out of MVP), so the shipped SFX scope (§7.3) is not disturbed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1 — New chapter file created:** An **AI Hell Music System** chapter is saved as a Markdown GDD addendum at `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md`. Its **musical substance** is taken from the producer's original *Music & Thematic Audio Design* brief (Phrygian Dominant + Lydian scales; Combat Motifs A and B and the ambient "Star Drift" motif; the combat, boss and ambient progressions; the FM 2–4 operator + chiptune implementation notes — reproduced under **Source material (A)** below) and laid out in the **8-section + 2-appendix** professional structure of the approved reference brief (Ross, v1.0, 16 October 2026): **1** Audio Vision Statement; **2** Musical Identity (2.1 Tonal Language, 2.2 Core Motifs, 2.3 Chord Progressions); **3** Instrumentation Palette; **4** Dynamic Mixing Rules; **5** State-Driven Music Transitions (5.1 Transition Design Principles, 5.2 Transition Matrix, 5.3 Stinger System); **6** Implementation Guidelines (6.1 Audio Middleware, 6.2 Music Event Architecture, 6.3 Parameter Mapping Table, 6.4 Technical Specifications, 6.5 Audio Budget Table); **7** Composer and Sound Designer Briefs (7.1 Composer Brief, 7.2 Sound Designer Brief); **8** Audio Accessibility; **Appendix A** Motif Reference Sheet; **Appendix B** Glossary. The reference brief is a **structure exemplar only** — its Tableau card-game substance (D Dorian, harpsichord/cello ensemble, card-table SFX, parlour ambience) must **not** be imported into AI Hell's chapter.
- [ ] **AC2 — GDD §7.3 references the chapter:** The "Background Music" subsection in GDD §7.3 (Audio Direction) is updated to link the new chapter file, while retaining the explicit statement that background music is **out of MVP scope** (design reference only; SFX remains the only in-scope audio).
- [ ] **AC3 — GDD §8 future-scope row updated:** The "Background music" row in §8 (Future Scope) references the new chapter file so the doc stays self-consistent.
- [ ] **AC4 — Doc-only change, no behaviour impact:** No game code, SFX behaviour, or runtime audio pipeline is changed; existing §7.3 SFX scope and the shipped ToneForge pipeline remain authoritative for the MVP.
- [ ] **AC5 — Validation:** A new docs guard `src/audioDesignChapterDocs.test.ts` (following the sibling `*Docs.test.ts` convention, e.g. `src/powerUpWeaponRosterDocs.test.ts`) asserts, and passes, that: (i) `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` exists; (ii) it carries all 8 numbered sections plus Appendix A and Appendix B of the approved reference structure; (iii) GDD §7.3's "Background Music" subsection links the chapter **and** still states music is out of MVP scope; (iv) the GDD §8 "Background music" row links the chapter. All links resolve, and any index/table-of-contents entries are updated.
- [ ] **AC6 — Full project test suite must pass with the new changes** (docs-only; confirms no accidental code impact).

## Constraints

- Music remains **"design reference, out of MVP scope"** — no change to the existing scope stance in GDD §7.3 or §8.
- The chapter is a **synthesis**, not a verbatim import (Q4/Q5, this session): the **musical content** is the producer's original retro-arcade brief reproduced faithfully (Source material (A)); the **document structure** follows the approved reference brief (author: Ross; version 1.0; dated 16 October 2026 — Source material (B)). The reference brief's Tableau card-game substance is **not** carried over.
- Follow the repo's docs naming/style conventions where sensible (singular Markdown addendum under `docs/`, referenced by relative link).
- UK English throughout.

## Existing state

- GDD §7.3 "Audio Direction" covers MVP SFX: baked ToneForge WAV pipeline, SFX event catalogue, per-enemy/per-player audio character, beat-synced explosion accents, and a one-paragraph "Background Music" subsection stating music is a nice-to-have, out of MVP.
- GDD §8 "Future Scope" lists "Background music — Synthwave / retro electronic soundtrack" with no further detail.
- No existing work item implements or specifies background music; the work log contains no musical-identity design doc.

## Desired change

- Add the Audio Design Chapter (AI Hell musical content in the approved reference structure) as a standalone GDD addendum document.
- Point GDD §7.3's "Background Music" subsection and §8's future-scope row at the new document.
- Keep all gameplay/SFX/runtime behaviour untouched.

**Key Files:**
- `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` (new) — the Audio Design Chapter addendum (confirm filename at implementation)
- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — §7.3 "Background Music" subsection updated with a link + scope note; §8 "Background music" row updated with a link
- `src/audioDesignChapterDocs.test.ts` (new) — docs guard following the sibling `*Docs.test.ts` convention
- `./README.md` (if it indexes docs) — optional link to the new chapter

## Related work

- **Update GDD audio design section and code comments (AH-0MTGS9DZ6001IFJR)** — completed; historical GDD §7.3 SFX additions, unrelated to music direction.
- **Update audio documentation (AH-0MUTYV9QV0000HDT)** — completed; ToneForge baked-asset pipeline docs; source of the current §7.3 scope language.
- **Update GDD with Audio Design Chapter (AH-0MVAUUV1U005UM4W)** — this item.
- See also GDD §7.3 and §8, and `docs/AUDIO_TONEFORGE_CUE_MAPPING.md` for the authoritative SFX cue catalogue.

## Risks & assumptions

- **Scope-stance divergence (medium):** the chapter is "APPROVED FOR PRODUCTION" in tone while the GDD keeps music out of MVP. Mitigated by AC2/AC3 explicitly framing the chapter as design reference; implementation remains a future work item.
- **Middleware references (FMOD/Wwise) are forward-looking:** the game currently uses Phaser/Web Audio with baked assets (§7.3). The chapter's §9 middleware guidance is design intent for future integration, not an instruction to adopt FMOD/Wwise in the MVP. Noted in the chapter context if needed.
- **Content divergence from shipped SFX:** the chapter (§6.4) proposes procedural SFX recipes that differ from the shipped baked-ToneForge SFX catalogue. The chapter is an addendum; §7.3 remains authoritative for MVP SFX (per constraint). Recorded as an assumption.
- **Scope creep:** producer may later want chapter sections mapped into the live audio system — that is future implementation work, tracked separately, not part of this docs-only item.

## Appendix: clarifying questions & answers

- Q1: "Where in the GDD should the 'Music & Thematic Audio Design' content live? (a) replace the §7.3 'Background Music' paragraph with the full chapter; (b) keep the paragraph and add a new top-level section; (c) other." — Answer (user): "A — below is a full brief for the music. Use this to create a new file and refer to it from 7.3." Source: interactive reply. The final decision refines (a): rather than inlining, create a **new file** (`docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md`) and **refer to it from GDD §7.3**; adopted as AC1/AC2.
- Q2: "MVP scope statement for music — (a) keep music 'design reference, out of MVP scope'; (b) promote into MVP." — Answer (user): "A." Source: interactive reply. Adopted as the chapter's scope framing (AC2/AC3).

Music & Thematic Audio Design

This section defines the musical identity of the game, focusing on scales, motifs, harmonic language, and usage guidelines across gameplay states. The goal is to merge retro‑arcade space tension (Asteroids) with relentless survival energy (Vampire Survivors), using a coherent musical palette that supports procedural layering and dynamic intensity shifts.

🎼 1. Core Musical Identity

The soundtrack is built around two complementary scales:

Primary Combat Scale — Phrygian Dominant

Used for: wave combat, boss spawns, high‑intensity survival phases.

Scale Formula: 1 ♭2 3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7Example (E): E – F – G♯ – A – B – C – D

Why:

Retro‑arcade tension

Exotic, driving, instantly “space danger”

Works extremely well with FM bass, square leads, and arpeggiators

Provides strong melodic hooks with minimal notes

Secondary Ambient Scale — Lydian

Used for: menus, starfield travel, upgrade screens, low‑intensity exploration.

Scale Formula: 1 2 3 ♯4 5 6 7Example (C): C – D – E – F♯ – G – A – B

Why:

Bright, floating, cosmic

Contrasts the combat scale without breaking aesthetic cohesion

Ideal for pads, shimmering arps, and soft synth textures

🎵 2. Melodic Motifs

Motifs are intentionally short (2–6 notes) to support looping, procedural recombination, and chiptune‑style repetition.

Combat Motif A — “Incoming Wave”

Scale: Phrygian Dominant (E)Contour: Rising tension → abrupt dropNotes: E – F – G♯ – F – E – DUsage:

Triggered at the start of each enemy wave

Can be fragmented into E–F–G♯ for micro‑stingers

Works well as a 3‑note arpeggiated alert

Combat Motif B — “Survival Pulse”

Scale: Phrygian Dominant (E)Rhythmic Cell: Dotted + straightNotes: G♯ – A – G♯ – F – EUsage:

Mid‑combat loop

Easily reharmonized for intensity scaling

Can be doubled with FM bass for crunchy retro drive

Ambient Motif — “Star Drift”

Scale: Lydian (C)Contour: Floating, circularNotes: C – E – F♯ – E – D – CUsage:

Menu screens

Upgrade/shop interface

Slow arpeggiated background texture

🎹 3. Harmonic Progressions

Retro arcade music often avoids complex harmony, but these progressions provide structure while staying loop‑friendly.

Combat Progression (Phrygian Dominant)

E – F – E – D

Minimalist, modal, tense

Works with pulsing bass and rapid arps

Can be expanded to E – F – G♯ – F – E – D – C – D for boss phases

Boss Progression (Phrygian Dominant, extended)

E – C – D – F – E

Chromatic tension

Strong “danger escalation” feel

Supports heavy FM brass or distorted square leads

Ambient Progression (Lydian)

C – D – E – F♯

Bright, drifting, spacey

Works well with pads and slow-moving textures

Can be looped seamlessly or expanded to C – G – D – F♯

🔧 4. Implementation Notes

Motifs should be stored as atomic musical objects (interval sets + rhythm cells) for procedural recombination.

Combat layers should increase harmonic density (more voices, faster arps) rather than changing the motif.

Ambient layers should use long‑release envelopes and minimal rhythmic content.

FM synthesis (2–4 operators) and chiptune waveforms (square, triangle, noise) define the retro palette.

All motifs should be designed to loop cleanly at 1–2 bars for dynamic layering.

# Dev-mode write-back: gym "Save to repo" persists bot tuning to src/data/bot-tuning.json

**Priority:** medium · **Issue type:** feature

**discovered-from:** AH-0MV9GZD2C005IIU3 (its scope-creep note flagged this path out of scope there)

## Problem statement

Today the Bot Tuning gym persists only to `localStorage` (`ai-hell-bot-tuning`), and the Git-tracked shipped baseline `src/data/bot-tuning.json` must be refreshed manually via the gym **Export** button → overwrite file → commit (documented in `docs/BOT_FRAMEWORK.md` §12 and `docs/dev/gameplay-capture.md`). Player ship and enemy/difficulty configs already have a dev-mode write-back path: the Vite CSV plugin (`vite/plugins/configCsvPlugin.ts`, served `/api/csv/...` PUT endpoints) writes gym Save/Save-As edits straight into the committed CSVs (`src/core/configStore.ts` `saveShipConfig`/`saveEnemyConfig`). This item gives bot tuning the same convenience: a dev-mode (Vite-serve-only) write path that persists the currently-selected tuning configuration to `src/data/bot-tuning.json`, so a designer does not have to Export → overwrite → commit manually.

## Users

- Designer tuning the demo bot in the Bot Tuning gym — wants a Save action that writes current tuning back to the committed baseline (dev server only).
- Maintainer / release reviewer — wants the write path dev-only and explicit, so a production/static build can never mutate the committed baseline.

Example user stories:

- *As a designer tuning the demo bot, I want a Save action in the Bot Tuning gym to write my current tuning back to `src/data/bot-tuning.json` (dev server only), so the shipped baseline stays in sync without the manual Export → overwrite → commit dance.*
- *As a maintainer, I want the write path to be dev-only and explicit, so a production/static build can never mutate the committed baseline or surprise a distributed user.*

## Desired change

1. **Write endpoint** — expose a dev-only endpoint (e.g. `PUT /api/bot-tuning/`) in the Vite dev-server plugin chain, mirroring the `configCsvPlugin` pattern (allowed-path allowlist, atomic write = temp file + rename, `apply: 'serve'` only). The endpoint validates the incoming blob's shape before writing (reuse the store's `parseState`-style validation / `coerceTuningValues`) and writes the exact `serialiseBotTuningState()` JSON blob to `src/data/bot-tuning.json`.
2. **Gym affordance** — add a "Save to repo" (dev-only) button in the Bot Tuning gym panel, next to Export, that posts the current store state to the endpoint and reports success/failure (`SaveResult`-shaped, like `saveShipConfig`). Disabled or hidden outside dev (`import.meta.env.DEV`, matching `saveShipConfig`'s `isDev()` gate).
3. **Out-of-scope guard** — no runtime behaviour change and no new write path in production; same guard contract as the CSV store (`WRITE_UNAVAILABLE` outside dev). Atomic replace must preserve the trailing-newline/pretty-print format the `bot-tuning.json` tests expect (`src/data/bot-tuning.test.ts` asserts byte-identity with the store Export plus trailing newline).
4. **Tests** — unit tests for the write helper (valid blob replaces file; invalid blob rejected without touching the file; non-dev returns unavailable; byte round-trip with `serialiseBotTuningState()`), gym-level test that "Save to repo" calls the write path and reflects a real file write, and a plugin-endpoint test mirroring `vite/plugins/configCsvPlugin.test.ts` scope. `npm run typecheck` and the full suite stay green; the gym↔game duplicate-body parity guard stays green.

## Acceptance Criteria

- **AC1 — Dev-only write endpoint persists the baseline.** In dev mode, a write of the current `serialiseBotTuningState()` blob updates `src/data/bot-tuning.json` atomically; the file stays byte-identical to the store Export (pretty-print + trailing newline), so `src/data/bot-tuning.test.ts` round-trip tests pass after the write.
- **AC2 — Invalid input never corrupts the file.** A write with an invalid/unschematised blob fails with a clear `SaveResult` reason and leaves the committed file untouched.
- **AC3 — Production/static builds cannot write.** The endpoint is dev-serve-only and the client gate (`isDev()`) means a production build reports `WRITE_UNAVAILABLE` (no mutation of the shipped baseline).
- **AC4 — Gym affordance.** The Bot Tuning gym exposes a dev-only "Save to repo" control that persists the current selection and reports success/failure; hidden/disabled outside dev.
- **AC5 — Tests + validation.** Unit + gym + plugin-endpoint tests cover persistence, rejection, round-trip, and non-dev unavailability; `npm run typecheck`, the full suite, and the parity guard pass.

## Constraints

- No change to bot decision/permission semantics — only a dev-tool persistence path (same scope boundary recorded in AH-0MV9GZD2C005IIU3).
- Follows the CSV plugin precedent exactly (atomic write, allowed-path allowlist, `apply: serve` only); do not invent a new infra pattern.
- The stored file must stay Git-committable and byte-stable (test contract).
- Out of scope: automatic background sync on every slider move (that would spam writes); the affordance must be an explicit Save action.
- Out of scope: any write path in production/static builds; dev-only via Vite serve.

## Existing state

- `src/core/botTuningStore.ts` already exports `serialiseBotTuningState()` (the exact Export blob) and has `parseState`-style (private) schema validation + `coerceTuningValues` from `src/ai/tuningFields.ts`.
- `src/data/bot-tuning.json` is the Git-tracked baseline whose byte-format contract is pinned by `src/data/bot-tuning.test.ts` (pretty-print + trailing newline, byte-identical to fresh-profile Export).
- `vite/plugins/configCsvPlugin.ts` is the established dev-write infra: `apply: 'serve'`, `/api/csv/...` GET/PUT, atomic write helper, allowed-path allowlist; registered in `vite.config.ts`.
- `src/core/configStore.ts` defines the `SaveResult` / `WRITE_UNAVAILABLE` / `isDev()` contract the bot-tuning write should mirror.
- `src/scenes/gym/GymBotTuning.ts` already has the Export button/status readout in `_buildActionRow()` and the panel-status helpers; a "Save to repo" button slots in alongside.

## Key Files (predicted)

- `vite/plugins/configCsvPlugin.ts` — the CSV dev-write pattern to parallel/clone for bot tuning
- `vite/plugins/configCsvPlugin.test.ts` — the plugin-endpoint test harness to mirror
- `src/core/botTuningStore.ts` — `serialiseBotTuningState()`, `parseState`/`coerceTuningValues` validation, `BOT_TUNING_SCHEMA_VERSION`
- `src/core/configStore.ts` — `saveShipConfig`/`saveEnemyConfig` + `SaveResult`/`WRITE_UNAVAILABLE` contract to mirror
- `src/data/bot-tuning.json` — the committed baseline the dev write targets
- `src/data/bot-tuning.test.ts` — file round-trip/trailing-newline contract the writer must preserve
- `src/scenes/gym/GymBotTuning.ts` — new "Save to repo" control next to Export
- `src/scenes/gym/GymBotTuning.test.ts` — gym-level write-path test
- `vite.config.ts` — plugin registration
- Docs: `docs/BOT_FRAMEWORK.md` §12, `docs/dev/gameplay-capture.md` — update the refresh workflow (dev write vs Export)

## Related work

- `Distributed versions of the game do not use the correct Bot definitions (AH-0MV9GZD2C005IIU3)` — completed; introduced the bundled baseline this write-back refreshes; its scope-creep note explicitly deferred this dev-mode write path.
- `Gym scene for AI bot tuning (AH-0MV4D7LAD009XYR0)` — completed; the tuning gym + store.
- `Watch Demo and video recording should fly the saved bot-tuning configuration (AH-0MV6MFDYG001E6PL)` — completed; Export/`--bot-config` workflow.
- `Config store: in-memory registry, boot load, dev write (AH-0MUE2MGZM0016U3L)` / `Vite CSV plugin: dev middleware (GET/PUT, atomic write, validation) (AH-0MUE2MHRC0090AXP)` — completed; the CSV write-back precedent this item parallels.

## Risks & assumptions

- **Assumption — "Save to repo" writes the full store state** (`serialiseBotTuningState()` blob, all named configs + current selection), i.e. exactly the Export blob. This is the only format the byte-identity test contract accepts (the shipped file is the whole `{ version, current, configs }` state), so the button's "current selection" phrasing means the current exported state. (If instead only the single selected config should be written, the file-format contract would need revisiting — not expected.)
- **Assumption — endpoint shape** follows the CSV-plugin precedent: a dev-only Vite middleware, PUT `/api/bot-tuning/` (or a parallel path under a bot-tuning prefix), validating before atomic write. Exact path is an implementation decision within the pattern.
- **Risk — stale baseline:** unchanged existing risk; the dev write reduces (does not eliminate) manual-drift by making the refresh an explicit action.
- **Risk — surprise writes:** a designer clicking Save expects a repo mutation; mitigations: dev-only gate, explicit button label + tooltip, `SaveResult` feedback.
- **Scope-creep risk:** automatic background sync on every slider move is out of scope (explicit Save only). Record any follow-up ideas as new work items, not scope.

## Verification of existing information

- Verified in repo: `serialiseBotTuningState()` is exported from `src/core/botTuningStore.ts` (byte-identical Export blob); `coerceTuningValues` exported from `src/ai/tuningFields.ts`; `parseStateObject` is private (a small store change or a plugin-local validator may be needed — implementation detail, not a requirement change).
- Verified in repo: `configCsvPlugin` exports `atomicWrite`, uses `apply: 'serve'`, allowed-path allowlist, and its test suite exercises PUT/atomic/validation via a real ephemeral HTTP server with `serve`/`build` modes — the exact harness to mirror.
- Verified in repo: `GymBotTuning._buildActionRow()` already builds Export + status; `GymPlayer._onSave()` shows the `saveShipConfig` status-reporting pattern to mirror.
- Duplicate check performed — no overlapping item found (searches: "write-back", "save to repo", "config write"; the closest completed items are the CSV write-back precedent and the scoped-out parent note).

## Appendix: Clarifying questions & answers

- Q: None required — the seed context (detailed discovered-from description) sufficed to draft a clear brief; the repo confirms the referenced APIs and file-format contract. Assumptions above are flagged for producer confirmation rather than asked, per the intake rule to not ask answerable-by-repo questions.
- Open question (advisory, not blocking): endpoint shape — preferred option **parallel dev-only middleware mirroring `configCsvPlugin`** (explicit path, keeps CSV plugin untouched and its tests stable); alternative is extending the CSV plugin's allowlist (rejected: not a CSV, and would complicate the CSV plugin's schema).

As the automated-balancing maintainer, I want `--batch` to automatically exercise the full shipped campaign, so the default report reflects what players experience without extra flags.

## Acceptance criteria

- **AC1:** `--batch` and `--games N` with no extra flags play full campaigns and the report shows non-zero `waveReached`/`levelReached`/`upgradesSelected` distributions.

## Problem

`implement.py parent` decides whether a child worktree contains work via `_git_path_has_changes()` (`skill/implement/scripts/implement.py`), whose docstring says it returns True when the worktree HEAD *differs* from the parent branch. A child worktree that is merely **behind** `dev` (HEAD != `dev`, but zero commits ahead and no dirty files) is therefore classified as "has changes" and `phase_parent` immediately runs `finish` on it.

Observed 2026-10-19 during the AH-0MVF3BESP005ZDAV epic:

1. `implement.py drive` started child AH-0MVF6XLBQ002GYWQ and its session was killed at the 3600 s timeout with a clean worktree (no edits, no commits).
2. While the drive was running, three unrelated commits landed on `dev`, so the child worktree was 3 commits behind.
3. `implement.py parent` reported `Child AH-0MVF6XLBQ002GYWQ has changes — running finish subprocess...` and ran `finish` on empty work. `finish`'s changed-scope selection was unavailable and fell back to a full-suite run (~10 min under load), which failed and reported `Failed to finish child`.

## Expected behaviour

A worktree with no dirty files and **no commits ahead of** the parent branch must be treated as "no work" (return the child as `next_child` for implementation), regardless of how far behind it is. The worktree placement guard should likewise not be affected.

## Suggested fix

- In `_git_path_has_changes()`, replace the "HEAD differs from parent branch" test with an ahead-count test (`git rev-list --count <parent>..HEAD` > 0) so behind-only worktrees are clean.
- Add a regression test covering: clean worktree at the fork base, clean worktree behind `dev`, dirty worktree, worktree with one commit ahead.

## Acceptance Criteria

- **AC1:** A child worktree with no uncommitted changes and no commits ahead of the parent branch is not treated as having changes by `phase_parent` (covered by a unit test).
- **AC2:** A child worktree that is behind `dev` but has no local commits does not trigger a `finish` subprocess.
- **AC3:** Worktrees with commits ahead, or with dirty files, are still detected as having changes (no regression).

## Problem

`node_modules/.vite` accumulates orphaned `deps_temp_<hash>` directories whenever a Vite dep optimisation is interrupted or collides — at intake there were 98 (141 MB), now **95 dirs / 158 MB total in `node_modules/.vite`**. They are pure cache debris: each is a partially written pre-bundle. The epic's AC3 timing work is unaffected functionally, but the debris wastes disk, slows directory scans, and is evidence that dep optimisation is re-running/colliding (which is one source of the transform/import variance measured in AH-0MVF6Y29M005TEOG).

## Why this was not fixed inline

`node_modules` is **shared by every worktree on this host via symlink**; deleting the cache while another agent's suite is mid-run can corrupt that run. The producer rule 'never destroy another agent's work' applies, so the cleanup needs a safe, quiescent mechanism rather than an opportunistic `rm -rf`.

## Expected change

A small, documented, safe cleanup path — e.g. `scripts/clean-vite-cache.mjs` that:
- refuses to run when any `vitest`/`vite` process is alive (or requires `--force`),
- removes only `deps_temp_*` (never the valid `deps/` bundle or `deps_ssr`),
- reports bytes reclaimed, and
- is documented in `docs/dev/test-suite-timing.md` (cache-hygiene section) and optionally wired into `scripts/hygiene_check.sh`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- **AC1:** A read-only `--dry-run` (default) reports the orphaned `deps_temp_*` count and bytes; `--apply` removes only those dirs and prints the reclaimed bytes.
- **AC2:** The script refuses to delete while a `vitest`/`vite` process is running unless `--force` is passed, and is covered by tests (dry-run classification, refusal path) that do not require a real cache.
- **AC3:** Documentation states why the cache is shared across worktrees and why the quiescence guard exists.
- **AC4:** After `--apply` on an idle host, `npx vitest run --project unit` still passes (cache regenerates cleanly).

# evaluate.mjs --tune: fail fast on unwritable --out and survive hard kill without dirty CSV

## Summary
During the 2026-10-21 end-to-end tune-loop verification (AH-0MVBNLM2V008XC8T), the negative-probe command

  node scripts/evaluate.mjs --tune --set enemy-configs.csv boss.health=7 --games 2 --ticks 200 --out /proc/nope/x

hung for 166.6 minutes inside a single Pi bash call before being killed (exit 137 / SIGKILL) — the largest
single tool call of the day (2.8 h of ~11.8 h active agent time). Instead of failing fast on the unwritable
output path, the CLI runs both sweeps first and validates the output directory only at write time. A hard
kill also means the in-memory CSV restore in the finally block cannot run: the session log shows the CSV
dirty (M src/data/enemy-configs.csv, changed md5) immediately after the kill (clean now, restored by later
session activity). Root cause to confirm during implementation; hypotheses: (a) output-dir validation
happens only after the sweeps, (b) no internal watchdog/timeout on the sweep, (c) SIGKILL (OOM/timeout)
skips the finally-based restore, (d) the pipe to tail can mask the true exit.

## User stories
- As a developer running tune-loop verification I want --tune to validate --out (and the CSV path) up-front
  so an invalid path fails in seconds, not hours.
- As a developer I want the tune/edit cycle crash-safe so even a hard kill never leaves the balance CSV
  edited in the worktree.

## Suggested approach
1. Validate options.outputDir and src/data/<tuneFile> before booting the SSR core or running any batch:
   a quick mkdir/writeability probe with a clear message and non-zero exit (ideally < 2 s).
2. Make edit/restore crash-safe: persist a small journal (target path + original bytes) beside the CSV
   before editing; restore/reconcile from the journal on next invocation (and document a manual repair
   path); do not rely solely on an in-memory finally.
3. Add a bounded-runtime watchdog or per-phase progress output for the sweep so an abnormal run cannot
   stall silently for hours; 2x200-tick games should take minutes, not hours.
4. Confirm the root cause with a repro before fixing (see hypotheses above); verify the observed exit code
   and CSV state in the repro.

## Acceptance criteria
1. The repro command above fails fast (< 2 s) with a clear "output directory not writable" diagnostic and
   a non-zero exit; demonstrated before and after the fix.
2. --tune with a valid --out still runs baseline -> edit -> re-run -> compare -> restore and exits 0;
   existing behaviour is preserved and existing evaluate/tune tests stay green.
3. A simulated hard kill (SIGKILL) at any point after the edit leaves the CSV byte-identical to the pre-run
   state, or a deterministic, documented repair path restores it exactly.
4. The full verification command used in AH-0MVBNLM2V008XC8T (including the negative probe) completes
   without hanging; the CLI help/docs mention the new validation.
5. Unit tests cover the writeability probe, the journal/restore under simulated kill, and the CLI exit
   codes; run under the project test policy (test skill).

## Context and references
- scripts/evaluate.mjs: main(), executeTune(), applyCsvEditFile(), restoreCsvFile()
- Related work items: AH-0MVBNITA0005VQGN (--tune CLI), AH-0MVBNISWE009QFBL (CSV edit guaranteed restore),
  AH-0MVBNLM2V008XC8T (end-to-end tune-loop verification, where this was observed)
- Observed in session 2026-10-21T12-15-12-077Z (finding #2 of the session-time analysis)

# Enemy force fields scale with level progression

**Headline:** Add data-driven enemy force fields that appear from a per-archetype
start level (some enemies shielded from level 2, others later) and grow stronger
with each level, absorbing a number of player hits before the ship inside is
exposed and destroyed as normal.

## Problem statement

Deeper campaign levels currently raise threat only through raw enemy density and
firepower; each regular enemy is still a single-hit (or fixed 5-hit) target. The
result is that upgraded weapons trivialise late-level fodder. Adding a
**force-field layer** — a distinct, readable barrier that absorbs several hits
before the ship inside becomes vulnerable — gives the late campaign a new
escalation axis that existing durability (`EnemyConfig.health`) does not provide,
without touching weapon/power-up economies.

## Users

- **As a player**, I want enemies in deeper levels to absorb a few hits behind a
  visible barrier, so late-game firepower is challenged again and reading a
  shielded enemy (barrier first, hull second) is intuitive.
- **As a balance engineer**, I want force-field strength (which archetypes are
  shielded, from which level, and how the field's hit count grows) to be
  data-driven and tunable per enemy, so I can shape difficulty without scene
  code.
- **As a developer**, I want the force-field logic to live once in the shared
  core so the game and every gym behave identically, with no divergent copies.

## Acceptance Criteria

- **AC1 — Data-driven per-archetype fields.** New `EnemyConfig` fields
  `forceFieldStartLevel` (campaign level at which this archetype first gains a
  field; `0` = never shielded), `forceFieldStartHits` (field hits when it
  appears) and `forceFieldMaxHits` (field hits at the campaign maximum level)
  are added to the CSV schema/codec, config types and seed defaults, each
  defaulting so that **every existing enemy is unshielded at level 1** and the
  shipped campaign is behaviourally unchanged until at least level 2. Field
  strength at any level is `clamp(round(lerp(startHits @ startLevel → maxHits @
  10)), 0, 5)` via a pure, Phaser-free shared resolver. Heavier archetypes
  (Tank/Harvester) carry higher base values than light ones.
- **AC2 — Force-field absorbs hits before the hull.** A shielded enemy survives
  its fleet of field hits first; each absorbed hit consumes the bullet (with
  feedback) but does **not** decrement `EnemyConfig.health`. Only after the
  field is broken does the enemy's normal health apply (so most archetypes die
  on the next hit; the 5-HP Harvester still needs 5). Every player damage source
  (normal bullet, piercing, AOE weapons, Smart Bomb, Orbital Strike, Frenzy
  bonus hits) depletes the field through the existing shared `takeDamage()`
  seam — no parallel damage path. Player contact/ram behaviour is unchanged
  (both sides still destroyed on collision; the field does not absorb rams).
- **AC3 — Readable feedback.** Shielded enemies render a shared bubble drawn by
  the `CombatEffectVisuals` helper family, visually distinct from the player's
  Shield and Force Field bubbles; each absorbed hit triggers the existing shared
  impact feedback; the breaking hit runs a distinct break flash/audio cue.
- **AC4 — Gym parity and tunability.** The same resolver drives the game
  (`PlayScene` spawn path, run level from `WaveManager`) and the level gym
  (`GymLevel`), with a parity test. The enemy-config gym editor
  (`GymFodderEnemies` slider surface) gains force-field controls so a
  formation-gym (no campaign context) spawn can force a field on with a given
  hit count; the divergence (gym slider sets hits directly instead of a level
  curve) is recorded in the code and this item.
- **AC5 — Verification and documentation.** Unit tests cover the resolver curve
  (start level, ramp, clamping, cap, L1-unchanged), CSV codec defaults, entity
  absorb/break behaviour, and scene integration; game↔gym parity test passes;
  the duplicate-body guard stays green; a bot-batch evidence run at L1/L5/L10
  records `survivalSeconds`, `levelReached`, `avoidableHits` and
  `enemiesKilledByArchetype` before/after (or demonstrates the field keeps the
  campaign playable). GDD §2.6 (remove "no shield layer"), §4.1 and
  `docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md` are updated with the new behaviour
  and tuning table; **all related documentation is updated** and the **full
  project test suite passes** with the changes.

## Constraints

- **Gym↔game parity is mandatory** (repo `AGENTS.md`): enabled gameplay
  behaviour is shared code consumed by the game and every relevant gym; only a
  documented disabled feature may diverge. The force-field resolver and bubble
  helper must live in the shared core, not per-scene copies.
- **Level 1 is untouched.** Defaults guarantee zero shielded enemies at level 1,
  preserving onboarding, tests and the existing balance baseline.
- **No changes to enemy `health`, weapon/power-up economies, or the player
  Force Field / Shield power-ups.** Fields are a new, additive layer.
- **Backwards-compatible config persistence** — existing enemy config blobs and
  the CSV load with the new fields defaulted (`0`); no schema break.
- **Determinism** — field strength is a pure function of (level, config); same
  level + seed ⇒ identical shields, so the fixed/curve campaign determinism
  contract is preserved.
- **No new player-facing UI** beyond the in-game bubble and gym editor controls.

## Existing state

- Regular-enemy health is data-driven (`EnemyConfig.health`, default 1; Harvester
  5 HP) and applied via `BaseEnemy.takeDamage()` — the shared damage seam every
  damage source already routes through (`src/scenes/core/CombatScene.ts`:
  bullet, piercing, AOE, Smart Bomb, Orbital Strike, Frenzy).
- `EnemyConfig` is CSV-backed (`src/data/enemy-configs.csv`) with a numeric
  codec (`src/core/csv.ts`), seed defaults (`src/core/configDefaults.ts`) and a
  **gym enemy editor** slider surface (`GymFodderEnemies.ENEMY_SLIDER_RANGES`).
- Spawn seam: `PlayScene._spawnEnemy` → `loadEnemyConfig(key)` →
  `createEnemyFromConfig`; the run level is available via `WaveManager.level`.
  `GymLevel` launches real campaign waves through the same factory.
- The **player** has Shield (absorbs hits) and Gradius-style Force Field
  (reflects bullets) power-ups; neither has any enemy-side counterpart. GDD
  §2.6 currently states "no shield layer", which this feature deliberately
  changes.
- Level-scaling work is in flight (epic AH-0MVHT1M6O003PU7P): its contract tests
  (AH-0MVLJCYGW001TRB3) are done; the `src/core/levelScaling.ts` implementation
  (`AH-0MVLJEE7O008RX9X`) is pending.

## Desired change

1. Add `forceFieldStartLevel` / `forceFieldStartHits` / `forceFieldMaxHits` to
   `EnemyConfig` (types, CSV codec, seed defaults, CSV rows; default 0/1/1).
2. Add a pure resolver (proposed `src/core/enemyForceField.ts`,
   `enemyForceFieldHits(level, config)`); coordinate reuse of
   `levelScaling.ts` plumbing if F1 (AH-0MVLJEE7O008RX9X) has landed.
3. Thread the resolved field hits into entity spawn (game and level gym through
   the shared factory/config path) and implement field state + bubble in
   `BaseEnemy` (draw, absorb decrement, break effects); keep `takeDamage()`
   consuming the field before `health`.
4. Add the shared bubble/break visuals to `CombatEffectVisuals` and any new SFX
   cue to the audio registry; add the gym-editor force-field sliders.
5. Tests: TDD contract tests for the resolver/codec/entity, game↔gym parity,
   and a bot-batch evidence run at L1/L5/L10.
6. Update GDD §2.6/§4.1 and `docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md`; refresh
   the enemy-config CSV header comments.

## Key Files

- `src/core/configTypes.ts` — Add `forceFieldStartLevel`, `forceFieldStartHits`, `forceFieldMaxHits` to `EnemyConfig`.
- `src/core/configDefaults.ts` + `src/data/enemy-configs.csv` — Seed defaults and per-archetype values (`0` default = never/unchanged).
- `src/core/csv.ts` — Numeric codec support for the new columns (default 0).
- `src/core/enemyForceField.ts` — **New** pure resolver `enemyForceFieldHits(level, config)` (curve, clamp, cap 5, L1 = 0).
- `src/entities/BaseEnemy.ts` — Field state, bubble draw, absorb-before-health in `takeDamage()`, break feedback.
- `src/entities/enemyFactory.ts` — Thread effective field hits into entity construction from config.
- `src/scenes/PlayScene.ts` — Resolve and pass field hits at spawn (run level via `WaveManager`).
- `src/scenes/gym/GymLevel.ts` (+ `GymBotTuning`/`GymCurveSequencer` if they spawn campaign waves) — same resolver for parity.
- `src/scenes/gym/GymFodderEnemies.ts` — Force-field sliders/controls on the enemy-config editor (documented divergence: direct hits, no level curve).
- `src/scenes/core/CombatEffectVisuals.ts` (+ tests) — Shared enemy-force-field bubble + break flash helper.
- `src/audio/effects.ts` — Any field-break cue (reuse existing cues where possible).
- `src/scenes/core/CombatScene.equivalence.test.ts` — Game↔gym parity block stays green.
- `src/core/*.test.ts`, `src/entities/BaseEnemy.test.ts`, `src/scenes/PlayScene.test.ts`, `src/scenes/gym/*.test.ts` — Resolver, codec, entity, integration tests.
- `src/ai/eval/` + `scripts/evaluate.mjs` — Bot-batch evidence mode at L1/L5/L10 (extend the F5 per-level harness if landed).
- `docs/Game Design Document.md`, `docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md` — Behaviour + tuning table.

## Related work

- **AH-0MVHT1M6O003PU7P** (in-progress epic) — Level-scaled enemy counts / power-up drops; the level-scaling infrastructure (`levelScaling.ts`, F1 AH-0MVLJEE7O008RX9X) that this feature coordinates with.
- **AH-0MUI820PM0038HS2** (completed) — Harvester + data-driven multi-hit `health`; the seam this feature extends.
- **AH-0MUJRVYWG006NJUU** (completed) — Shared multi-hit kill finalisation / `takeDamage` seam.
- **AH-0MUJRVYJH00485YR** (completed) — Data-driven enemy health config (CSV codec + editor).
- **AH-0MTV7JOLU006W8PT** (completed) — Contact rule: player crashing into an enemy destroys both (unchanged by this item).
- **AH-0MVBKT2WO001AR14** (open) — Player Force Field feedback (distinct scope; do not conflate).
- **AH-0MV97RISJ002WR2S** (open) — Wave Laser limited hit power (piercing interplay; verify AOE/piercing behaviour against the field).
- Repo `AGENTS.md` — Gym↔game parity convention.

### Related work (automated report)

#### Related work items
- **AH-0MT7USMWN0071UF5** – Clarify enemy pass-through and bullet-blocking rules in GDD (Wall vs Dive Bomb) (completed)
- **AH-0MVBKT2WO001AR14** – More forcefield feedback (open)
- **AH-0MU7JTEY3004EXR2** – Show level/wave progress as 'Level N of 5, Wave M of K' (completed)

#### Repository file matches
- `docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md` — matched: destroyed, enemies, exposed, fields, force (+13 more); the enemy-build/health seams this feature extends
- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — matched: the GDD §2.6/§4.1 floor the "no shield layer" rule this item changes
- `README.md` — matched: broad gameplay terms; check for any shield/level claims on release

## Risks & Assumptions

- **Assumption:** the three-field linear model (start level, start hits, max hits at L10) is the right "per-enemy curve variation" shape; operator confirmed per-enemy tunable start levels (some L2, others L3+) and "subtle variations of this curve for different enemies".
- **Assumption:** "killed in a single hit" after field break applies to the 1-HP majority; the Harvester keeps its 5 HP once its field is down (AC2, operator Q2 = A).
- **Assumption (flagged for review):** enemy fields absorb only player **bullet** damage; player **contact/ram** behaviour is unchanged (both destroyed, AH-0MTV7JOLU006W8PT). If shields should also protect against rams, that is a deliberate product change — call it out.
- **Risk:** force fields stack with the level-scaling density/drop changes (epic AH-0MVHT1M6O003PU7P) and could push late levels into bullet-sink tedium; mitigated by the 5-hit cap, per-archetype defaults, and bot-batch survival evidence.
- **Risk:** heavy archetypes (Tank/Harvester) with fields at L2–3 may frustrate players who maxed weapons; mitigated by keeping light archetypes unshielded for longer and tuning via CSV.
- **Risk:** the gym slider for formation gyms bypasses the level curve, so an editor could author values the campaign never produces; documented divergence + editorial note in the gym panel.
- **Risk:** editing the CSV schema/editor touches shared tooling (codec, gym panel, docs tests); keep defaults `0` so existing rows and persisted blobs load unchanged.
- **Scope-creep guard:** no retuning of enemy health, weapon levels, drop rates or the player shield/force-field power-ups; separate items are created for any of those discovered during implementation.

## Appendix: Clarifying questions & answers

- **Q1 — Which enemies gain a field, and how does it scale with level?** Options: (A) one global level curve for all regular ships; (B) per-archetype data-driven `forceFieldHits` in the enemy CSV/editor plus a level bonus; (C) level-scaled spawn chance with a small fixed field; (D) only heavy archetypes. — **Answer (operator): B — "start with a heavier getting stronger fields".** Source: interactive reply. Per-archetype base values, with heavier/larger archetypes (Tank, Harvester) entitled to stronger fields; the level curve strengthens them further.
- **Q2 — Does the field replace or stack on existing health?** Options: (A) separate layer — field absorbs N hits first, then normal `EnemyConfig.health` (Harvester keeps 5 HP); (B) the field replaces durability — one hit after break, even the Harvester; (C) merge field + health into a single bubble/total. — **Answer (operator): A.** Source: interactive reply. Field is an additive layer in front of existing data-driven health.
- **Q3 — How much feedback and balance evidence?** Options: (A) full — shared bubble (distinct from player's), absorb flash, break flash/cue, gym control to force fields, level-gym parity, bot-batch evidence at L1/L5/L10; (B) bubble + flash only, no audio, no bot batch; (C) minimal body tint instead of a bubble. — **Answer (operator): A.** Source: interactive reply. Full feedback surface and balance evidence.
- **Q4 — Should heavy archetypes show a field at level 1, or only from a start level?** Options: (A) fields appear only from a start depth (level-1 run untouched), with the level curve adding field hits past level 2; (B) heavy archetypes show base field hits from level 1. — **Answer (operator): "This needs to be tunable on a per enemy basis, so some will have shields from level 2, others level 3 or more."** Source: interactive reply. Per-archetype `forceFieldStartLevel`; no field at level 1 for any archetype by default; some archetypes start at level 2, others later.
- **Q5 — Confirm the concrete level curve (L1–2: 0, L3–4: +1, L5–6: +2, L7–8: +3, L9–10: +4, base per archetype, cap 5).** Options: (A) adopt table; (B) bases all 0; (C) different shape. — **Answer (operator): "See 1 (use subtle variations of this curve for different enemies)."** Source: interactive reply. Adopted a three-field linear model — `forceFieldStartLevel`, `forceFieldStartHits`, `forceFieldMaxHits` (at level 10), `clamp(round(lerp), 0, 5)` — giving each archetype a subtle per-enemy variation of the reference curve.
- **Open item carried to review (assumption, not yet confirmed):** enemy fields absorb only player **bullet** damage; player contact/ram behaviour is unchanged (both destroyed, AH-0MTV7JOLU006W8PT). If shields should absorb rams too, that is a product change to confirm during brief review.

## Goal

Crash resilience for dev telemetry: with the dev JSONL sink moving to an in-memory per-run buffer (AH-0MVIRYGD1000JVY3), a page reload or crash mid-run loses the un-uploaded tail. Streaming telemetry batches to the dev server during the run — instead of one run-end upload — bounds that loss to at most one flushed batch (~64 records, ~1.3 s of play) and removes the page-reload regression that localStorage previously masked.

## Context

- Parent/related: discovered-from:AH-0MVIRYGD1000JVY3 (in-memory dev sink; this item is explicitly deferred there).
- Current flow: the JsonlTelemetrySink buffers records in memory, flushes batches of 64 to the sink, and the whole run is POSTed once at run end (`uploadDevTelemetry`). A crash before that POST loses the entire run's telemetry; a reload also loses the buffer entirely once it is no longer localStorage-backed.
- Dev only: the same reasoning applies to the production remote sink, which already streams batches via `HttpTelemetryTransport` (with retry/backoff), so production is not affected.

## Proposed design

- Send each flushed batch to the dev endpoint as it is produced (`POST /api/telemetry/upload`) instead of (or in addition to) the run-end upload.
- The server (`vite/plugins/telemetryUploadPlugin.ts`) currently stores each upload as one complete `session-<stamp>.jsonl` and runs the automatic evaluation per upload; a per-batch POST would create many tiny recordings and repeated evaluations. The endpoint (or a new `part` protocol) must therefore either:
  - append JSONL records to the run's open session file keyed by a run id/seed, and evaluate once at run end, or
  - keep the run-end upload and add a lightweight "heartbeat/checkpoint" mechanism that only recovers the tail on demand.
- UX/offline: batches sent while the dev server is unreachable should stay in the memory buffer (or a bounded queue) and be retried at run end; at most one batch may be lost on a hard crash.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: A mid-run crash/reload followed by a run-end state loses no more than one flushed batch (~64 records / ~1.3 s) of telemetry; the rest is recoverable from the dev server.
- AC2: The server session file for a run contains its records exactly once (no duplication from partial + final uploads), and the automatic evaluation still runs once per run.
- AC3: Dev CLI tooling (`record-session`, `capture-gameplay`, `verify-dev-telemetry`) continues to work unchanged in behaviour.
- AC4: Full project test suite passes.

## Status

Open decision item — parked until the in-memory sink (AH-0MVIRYGD1000JVY3) lands. Do not implement concurrently with that item in the same worktree.

# Implement the Music System defined by the Audio Design Chapter

## Goal

Build the runtime background-music system for AI Hell against the fixed design contract captured in
`docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` (produced by **Update GDD with Audio Design Chapter (AH-0MVAUUV1U005UM4W)**).

User story: *As a player, I want a dynamic, retro-arcade soundtrack that responds to combat intensity, so
that runs feel like the relentless survival experience the game is aiming for; and as a developer I want the
music engine driven by a documented parameter/state contract, so behaviour is testable and reproducible.*

> **Scope stance:** this is **future scope, out of MVP** (GDD §8). The MVP ships baked ToneForge SFX only
> (GDD §7.3), and §7.3 remains authoritative for SFX. This item must **not** be started until the design
> chapter exists and has been reviewed, and it must **not** promote music into the MVP without an explicit
> producer decision.

## Background

- AI Hell currently has **no background music** by design: GDD §7.3 keeps music out of MVP scope, and the
  player-fire grid is deliberately quantised to a **silent internal 80 BPM beat** (AH-0MUAYB8EH005RJ8B).
- SFX are build-time baked WAV assets rendered deterministically by ToneForge and played through Phaser's
  shared `AudioContext` (`src/audio/effects.ts`); the authoritative cue catalogue is
  `docs/AUDIO_TONEFORGE_CUE_MAPPING.md`.
- The Audio Design Chapter specifies the musical identity (Phrygian Dominant combat scale, Lydian ambient
  scale, Combat Motifs A/B, "Star Drift"), instrumentation palette, dynamic-mixing rules, state-driven
  transitions, parameter mapping, audio budget and accessibility requirements.

## Expected behaviour and outcomes

- A music system that plays layered/stemmed music driven by an explicit game-state parameter, with
  bar-boundary transitions, stingers, and ducking, as specified by the chapter.
- Music state follows gameplay (e.g. menu/attract, wave combat, boss, low-health tension, run end) with the
  transition rules and timings given in the chapter, and never disrupts the beat grid or the SFX mix.
- Reproducible, deterministic behaviour suitable for automated tests; no audio regressions to the shipped SFX
  pipeline.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1 — Contract traceable to the chapter:** every implemented music state, transition, stinger and
      mixing parameter traces to a named section of `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md`, recorded in a mapping
      table in the implementation docs.
- [ ] **AC2 — Musical content matches the documented identity:** the delivered cues/stems use the chapter's
      scales, motifs and progressions (Phrygian Dominant combat, Lydian ambient, Combat Motifs A/B,
      "Star Drift"), verified by an explicit audit table (motif → scale degrees → usage state).
- [ ] **AC3 — State machine implemented and tested:** transitions occur only at the documented boundaries
      (bar boundaries unless a stinger cut-in is specified), with unit tests covering each transition in the
      chapter's transition matrix, including invalid/reset paths.
- [ ] **AC4 — Dynamic mixing implemented:** ducking, per-layer volume targets and the priority tiers behave as
      specified; SFX intelligibility is preserved (music ducks under key SFX cues) and is covered by tests.
- [ ] **AC5 — Autoplay and accessibility compliance:** no audio before a user gesture (`AudioContext`
      resume discipline, GDD §7.3); the chapter's accessibility requirements (e.g. music/SFX independent
      volume, mute, and any reduction options) are implemented and documented.
- [ ] **AC6 — Budget met:** the shipped music respects the chapter's audio budget (memory, streaming,
      polyphony, layer count) on the supported targets, measured and recorded.
- [ ] **AC7 — Docs updated:** GDD §7.3 and §8 are updated to reflect the shipped music system, and
      `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` is marked as implemented for the sections that ship.
- [ ] **AC8 — No SFX regression:** the existing ToneForge baked-SFX pipeline and cue catalogue remain
      unchanged and their tests pass; any chapter §6.4 procedural SFX recipes are explicitly **not** adopted
      unless decisioned separately.
- [ ] **AC9 — Full project build and test suite pass.**

## Constraints

- **Blocked by** the docs item **Update GDD with Audio Design Chapter (AH-0MVAUUV1U005UM4W)** — this item
  must not begin before `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` exists.
- Music stays **out of MVP scope** until a producer decision promotes it (GDD §7.3, §8).
- Keep the gameplay SVG/vector aesthetic and retro-arcade palette of the chapter; UK English in all docs.
- §7.3 (baked ToneForge SFX) remains authoritative for SFX; the chapter is an addendum whose §6.4 procedural
  SFX recipes are design reference only.
- Prefer reusing the existing audio plumbing (`src/audio/effects.ts`, shared `AudioContext`, manifest-driven
  playback) over introducing new runtime dependencies; any middleware adoption (the chapter's FMOD/Wwise
  guidance) is a separate decision — the web build currently has no middleware.

## Approach (indicative)

1. Confirm scope with the producer (MVP vs post-MVP) and record the decision on this item.
2. Ingest the chapter into an implementation mapping table (state → parameter → cue/stem set → transition).
3. Decide the delivery mechanism (baked stems via ToneForge + `AudioContext` playback, per the existing
   pipeline) versus a runtime synthesiser; record the trade-off before coding.
4. Implement the music state machine and mixing layer behind a single facade, mirroring the existing SFX
   façade style; add unit tests per transition and per mixing rule.
5. Add accessibility controls and the autoplay guard; verify budget and measure on target hardware.
6. Update GDD §7.3/§8 and the chapter's implemented-sections marker.

**Key Files:**
- `docs/AUDIO_DESIGN_CHAPTER.md` — the design contract (prerequisite)
- `src/audio/effects.ts` — existing SFX façade / shared `AudioContext` plumbing to reuse
- `src/scenes/core/CombatCoreScene.ts` — where combat-state music parameters would be driven from
- `src/core/rules.ts` — game-rules config (including `beatBpm`) that music tempo must stay coherent with
- `src/audio/` — new music module + tests
- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — §7.3 and §8 updates

## Risks & assumptions

- **Overlap with the shipped silent beat grid (medium):** player fire is quantised to an internal 80 BPM beat.
  Music must be tempo-coherent with that grid or the two will fight; assume music tempo is either locked to
  `beatBpm` or documented as intentionally independent.
- **Chapter/SFX divergence (medium):** the chapter's §6.4 procedural SFX recipes differ from the shipped baked
  catalogue; §7.3 stays authoritative (AC8).
- **Middleware assumption (low):** the chapter's FMOD/Wwise guidance is forward-looking; no middleware exists in
  the web build, so it is design intent only.
- **Scope creep into MVP (medium):** music is out of MVP; promotion needs an explicit producer decision.

## Related work

- **Update GDD with Audio Design Chapter (AH-0MVAUUV1U005UM4W)** — prerequisite; produces the design contract.
- discovered-from:AH-0MVAUUV1U005UM4W
- GDD §7.3 (SFX, authoritative for MVP), GDD §8 (Future Scope — "Background music"), and
  `docs/AUDIO_TONEFORGE_CUE_MAPPING.md` (SFX cue catalogue).
- Beat grid / timing context: AH-0MUAYB8EH005RJ8B (beat-aligned fire grid), AH-0MV01HNLU008S5E3 (beat-timed
  explosion accents).

## Problem

`skill/implement/scripts/implement.py` `_resolve_implementation_order()` builds its in-degree count from **every** in-chain dependency edge, including edges whose blocker is **already terminal** (`completed`/`in_review`/`done`). A terminal blocker therefore still occupies a slot in Kahn's ready queue and gates when its dependents become ready.

## Observed impact (2026-10-23, epic AH-0MV8BUKFK003Z23S)

The epic's 8 children were ordered as:

`[TOOK(test-failure, done), 3X5M, MVIS(done), VDA9, 7NGZ, O53Z(done), K0V4, BAAN]`

because `K0V4` (juice impl, sortIndex 3000 — the *lowest* open child) has an outbound 'depends-on' edge to `O53Z` (its test-first contract child, sortIndex **8100**). Since `O53Z` was already `completed`, `K0V4` should have been ready immediately, but the sort only released it after `O53Z`'s turn near the end of the queue.

Consequences observed:

1. `implement.py parent AH-0MV8BUKFK003Z23S` never reached `K0V4`, even though its worktree contained a completed in-flight implementation — it returned 'start child VDA9' instead. The in-flight work had to be finished manually with `implement.py finish K0V4`.
2. The reported order is not 'blockers first' in any intuitive sense: a ready child was deferred behind unrelated children purely because its (finished) blocker had a high sortIndex.

## Expected behaviour

Terminal blockers must not gate readiness: a child whose in-chain blockers are all terminal is **ready**, regardless of where those blockers sort. Suggested fix: exclude terminal blockers from `in_degree` (treat them as already satisfied) — or collapse them out of the graph before the sort — so the ready queue is ordered by `(sortIndex, id)` over genuinely-unblocked children.

## Acceptance criteria

- A child whose in-chain blockers are all terminal is ordered by its own `sortIndex`, before non-ready children and irrespective of its blockers' `sortIndex`.
- A regression test in the implement-skill test suite covers the exact shape seen here (open child with low sortIndex depending on a completed child with high sortIndex) and asserts the open child is first in the resolved order.
- No change to cycle detection, cross-project external-blocker reporting, or the blocked-child guard.
- Existing implement-skill tests pass.
